title: Comparing and choosing
job: More, less, better — stating a preference
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The comparative is one shape and it does NOT bend: akbar for a man, a woman, one thing or many. After nine modules in which every adjective took an -a, that is a relief rather than a burden.
"Than" is min — the same word as M1's "from" from the level below, and this is its third job: origin, the phrase min faḍlika, and now comparison. Its row is L1-M1's and nothing here can take it.
The superlative is the SAME afʿal, put in front of an indefinite singular: akbar bayt, "the biggest house". English has -er and -est; Arabic has one shape and lets the position decide.
afʿal is a PATTERN, not a meaning. M3's aḥmar, azraq and aswad have the same shape and are colours — nothing is "redder" here. The root decides, and the pattern is shared.
ayy asks you to pick from a set, and it is a sibling of M7's ayna and M4's matā rather than a form of them.

sentences.cue: The house is bigger than the school

words.note: Built from the same three letters as M3's kabīr, on the afʿal pattern. It never bends: akbar for anything at all.

sentences.trap: min is "from" everywhere else in this course. Here it is "than", and its row is L1-M1's — this module opens nothing and points back.
sentences.sound: AK-bar, stressed at the front like every afʿal word.

variations.cue: The school is bigger than the house
variations.changed: the comparison turned round, and akbar does not move

variations.cue: The car is bigger than the bus
variations.changed: two feminine nouns, and still akbar
the second thing left unsaid

mistake.why: There is no akbara. The comparative is invariable, which is the module's first and best news.

sentences.usage: The everyday comparison. The second variation is the one to notice: two feminine nouns and the adjective still does not move.

sentences.cue: She is older than my mother

words.note: M1's row from the level below, on its third job: origin in L1-M1, the phrase min faḍlika in L1-M8, and comparison here. First occurrence wins, so this module opens no row.

sentences.trap: akbar of a person is older, not bigger. The same word measures both, and the sentence says which.
sentences.sound: MIN, one short syllable, and identical in the script to M7's man.

variations.cue: He is older than my father
variations.changed: two men, and akbar again does not move

variations.cue: My mother is older than my father
variations.changed: two named people rather than a pronoun
min with a suffix, which is how it takes a pronoun

mistake.why: The word for than is min. an links two verbs and has no business here.

sentences.usage: Family talk, and the commonest use of akbar there is. Age in Arabic is a matter of size.
sentences.mnemonic: Bigger and older are one word.

sentences.cue: The train is faster than the bus

words.note: From M4's sarīʿ, on the same afʿal pattern as akbar. Seeing the pair together is how the pattern becomes usable rather than memorised.

sentences.trap: sarīʿ bends and asraʿ does not. The positive agrees and the comparative never does, which is the whole shape of the module.
sentences.sound: AS-raʿ, stressed at the front, with the ʿayn closing it.

variations.cue: The bus is faster than the car
variations.changed: the comparison turned round
M4's positive, which does agree
M4's advice with the reason after it

mistake.why: asraʿ is invariable. No comparative in Arabic takes an ending.

sentences.usage: Advice about how to get somewhere, which is M4's business finished properly.
sentences.mnemonic: The positive bends; the comparative stands still.

words.note: From M8's rakhīṣ in the level below, on the afʿal pattern. The kh and the ṣ are both made deep, so the word sits low in the mouth.

sentences.trap: The second thing is left unsaid, and Arabic is comfortable with that — the comparison is with whatever you are both looking at.
sentences.sound: AR-khaṣ, with the kh of "loch" and the ṣ emphatic.

variations.cue: This book is cheaper than this one
variations.changed: the second thing named with min
a feminine thing, and arkhaṣ does not move

variations.cue: the cheapest book in the market
variations.changed: in front of an indefinite noun, so it becomes a superlative

mistake.why: After hādhā the noun takes al-, as M5 taught: hādhā al-kitāb. Without it the phrase means "this is a cheaper book".

sentences.usage: In a market, holding two things. The third variation is the whole of S06 in miniature.
sentences.mnemonic: Behind a definite noun it compares; in front of an indefinite one it wins.

words.note: From M8's ghālī, and it ends in a long ā written with a dotless yāʾ — ى — which is a spelling a learner meets here for the first time.

sentences.trap: The pair to hold together: arkhaṣ and aghlā, cheaper and dearer, and neither of them bends.
sentences.sound: AGH-lā, with the gh a soft gargled g and a long open ā at the end.

variations.cue: This car is more expensive than the bus
variations.changed: the second thing named
a masculine thing, and aghlā does not move
M8's positive from the level below, which does agree

mistake.why: It ends in a plain long ā, written with the dotless yāʾ. There is no hamza on the end of it.

sentences.usage: The other half of a market conversation. Between arkhaṣ and aghlā a learner can shop.
sentences.mnemonic: Cheaper and dearer, and neither one bends.

sentences.cue: This is the biggest house in the market

words.note: M5's row from the level below, and here it is the GROUP the superlative picks from. Arabic marks the group with fī where English uses in.

sentences.trap: akbar bayt has no al- anywhere and means "THE biggest house". A comparative in front of an indefinite singular is a superlative, and that is the only signal.
sentences.sound: AK-bar BAYT, two stresses and no pause between them.

variations.cue: This is the cheapest book in the market
variations.changed: S04's word doing the same job

variations.cue: It's the biggest school in Egypt
variations.changed: a feminine noun, and the superlative still does not bend
with al- and behind the noun, which makes it a description again

mistake.why: The superlative takes no al- in front of its noun: akbar bayt. "Add al- for the superlative" is the rule to refuse.

sentences.usage: A claim rather than an opinion, which is what the fī-phrase adds.
sentences.mnemonic: No article, indefinite noun, and it is the best of them.

words.note: The same three letters as min faḍlika, the phrase the learner has been saying since L1-M8: a favour and a preference are one root.

sentences.trap: The thing preferred against takes ʿalā, "on". English says "to" and Arabic says "on", and neither is more logical than the other.
sentences.sound: u-FAḌ-ḍil, with the ḍ emphatic and doubled.

variations.changed: the preference turned round
asked, with the second thing left off

variations.cue: I prefer the train to the bus
variations.changed: M4's transport in the same frame

mistake.why: min is for a comparative adjective. ufaḍḍil takes ʿalā.

sentences.usage: Answering a choice, and the root it shares with min faḍlika is worth pointing out to a learner who has said that phrase a hundred times.
sentences.mnemonic: A favour and a preference come from one root.

words.note: Picks from a set both speakers can see. A sibling of M7's ayna and M4's matā rather than a form of them — they share a look and nothing else.

sentences.trap: The noun after ayy takes no al-. It is being picked from a set, not pointed at.
sentences.sound: AYY, one syllable with the y doubled and held.

variations.changed: the feminine address, which the script shows
the question and a comparative in four words
the answer, with S07's verb

mistake.why: After ayy the noun stays indefinite: ayy kitāb.

sentences.usage: A shop, a menu, a shelf. The answer is the sentence after it.
sentences.mnemonic: Picking from a set leaves the article off.

words.note: The afʿal of kathīran, M1's "a lot" from the level below. Its opposite is aqall, less, and both take min.

sentences.trap: akthar is a comparative of quantity and al-mazīd, which M5 taught, is a noun. They mean nearly the same thing and behave completely differently.
sentences.sound: AK-thar, with the th of "think" and the stress at the front.

variations.changed: the opposite, and it works identically

variations.cue: I have more than one car

M5's offer, in this module's word

mistake.why: akthar takes min, like every comparative in the module.

sentences.usage: At a table or a counter. The third variation is M5's offer said the other way round.

sentences.display: al-bayt al-aḥmar aṣghar min al-bayt al-kabīr
sentences.script: البيت الأحمر أصغر من البيت الكبير
sentences.cue: The red house is smaller than the big house
sentences.literal: The-house the-red smaller from the-house the-big

words.note: The opposite of akbar, on the same pattern and just as invariable. Its positive, ṣaghīr, is not taught in this course, which is why the comparative arrives first.

sentences.trap: al-aḥmar and aṣghar look like the same kind of word and are not. The first is a colour, the second a comparison, and they share a pattern — which is exactly what rule 3 said.
sentences.sound: AṢ-ghar, with the ṣ emphatic and the gh gargled.

variations.cue: The house is smaller than the school
variations.changed: without the colours
a feminine noun, and aṣghar still does not move

variations.cue: the smallest house in the market
variations.changed: the superlative, in front of an indefinite noun

mistake.display: al-bayt al-aḥmar aṣghar min al-bayt al-akbar
mistake.script: البيت الأحمر أصغر من البيت الأكبر
mistake.why: al-akbar is a comparison and not a description. The other house is simply big: al-bayt al-kabīr.

sentences.usage: The module's last sentence holds both readings of the afʿal pattern side by side, which is where rule 3 is either learnt or not.
sentences.mnemonic: Same shape, different jobs — and only the root knows which.
